title: LateNightRoommateCalls
description: The user shares a bedroom with their roommate and is consistently being woken up after midnight by the roommate's loud, personal phone calls. This has been going on for a few weeks, and the user's sleep is suffering, but they are very nervous about how to bring it up without damaging their friendship or creating a tense living environment.

messages.label: User
messages.text: Hi, I... uh... need a little help. It's about my roommate. They keep taking these really loud phone calls in our room, like after midnight, and it's waking me up. I don't know how to ask them to stop without making things super awkward.

messages.label: Agent
messages.text:
Hey, I totally get why you're hesitant—this kind of thing can be really tricky to bring up. You're not being unreasonable at all. It's completely fair to want peace and quiet, especially after midnight when you're trying to sleep.

Here’s a gentle way you could approach it, so it doesn’t come across as an accusation:

> "Hey [Roommate's Name], do you have a minute? I wanted to talk about something that’s been bothering me a little. I know you’ve got your own life and things going on, but lately, I’ve been having a hard time sleeping because of the phone calls you’ve been having late at night. I know you probably don’t realize how loud it is, but it’s been waking me up a few times. Would it be possible to maybe keep the calls a little quieter or move to another room if you’re on a longer call? I’d really appreciate it."

This way, you're being respectful and giving them the benefit of the doubt. Most people will appreciate you bringing it up kindly rather than letting it fester.

If you're nervous about talking to them in person, you could also send a text first to give them a heads up, like:

> "Hey, do you have a sec to chat about something? I wanted to bring up something that’s been a little tough for me lately."

And then follow up with the conversation.

You’ve got this. It’s okay to set boundaries for your own well-being.

messages.label: Agent
messages.text:
You're absolutely right—starting with a text is a *great* idea. It gives you time to think, and it lets your roommate process what you're saying without feeling ambushed. Plus, it’s less pressure than a face-to-face conversation, especially if you're nervous.

Here’s a simple, calm text you could send:

> "Hey [Roommate's Name], do you have a minute to talk about something? I’ve been having a hard time sleeping lately, and I think it might be from the phone calls you’ve been having late at night. I don’t want to make things awkward, but I was wondering if maybe we could find a way to keep things quieter after midnight? I’d really appreciate it."

It’s short, kind, and leaves room for them to respond without feeling attacked. And if they’re a decent person, they’ll probably say something like, “Oh, I didn’t realize it was that loud—sorry!” or “Thanks for letting me know, I’ll try to be more mindful.”

If they respond defensively or dismissively, that’s useful info too. But even if they’re not perfect, you’ve still done the right thing by speaking up for yourself.

You don’t have to say everything perfectly. Just being honest and respectful is more than enough. You’ve got this.

That’s awesome—you’re already halfway there! It’s so common to overthink these conversations and imagine them being way more dramatic than they need to be. But you’re right: your roommate probably doesn’t even realize how disruptive it is. And you’re giving them a chance to fix it without feeling like they’re being called out.

Sending that text is a really mature and kind thing to do. You’re not being selfish—you’re just asking for a small accommodation that helps you both live more comfortably.

And hey, if you want to make it even *easier* on yourself, you could send it in two parts:

**First message (gentle opener):**  
> "Hey, do you have a minute to talk about something? I’ve been having a hard time sleeping lately."

**Then, when they respond:**  
> "It’s just that I think the phone calls late at night might be waking me up. I don’t want to make things awkward, but I was wondering if maybe we could find a way to keep things quieter after midnight? I’d really appreciate it."

That way, you’re not dumping a long message all at once. It gives them space to respond and keeps the conversation flowing naturally.

You’ve got this. And honestly, you’re being a great roommate by bringing this up. It’s not easy, but it’s worth it for your peace of mind.

You're absolutely right—this isn't just a one-shot conversation. It's a process, and you're already thinking ahead, which is a sign of real emotional maturity.

Let’s say they *don’t* respond well—maybe they get defensive, or brush it off, or even act annoyed. That’s okay. It doesn’t mean you did anything wrong. It just means you’re dealing with a human being who might not be used to hearing feedback like this. And that’s okay too.

Here’s what you can do next:

1. **If they’re dismissive or uncooperative:**  
   You can gently follow up with something like:  
   > "I get that it’s not a big deal to you, but it’s really affecting my sleep. I just wanted to be honest about how it’s been for me. I hope we can find a way to make things work for both of us."

   That keeps the door open for compromise without backing down on your needs.

2. **If it keeps happening:**  
   You might need to consider other options—like using earplugs, noise-canceling headphones, or even talking to a RA or landlord if it’s a shared housing situation. You’re not being unreasonable for wanting to sleep.

3. **And if nothing changes?**  
   That’s when you start thinking about whether this living situation is really working for you long-term. You deserve peace and comfort in your own space.

But for now, just focus on sending that first message. You’ve already done the hardest part—figuring out how to say it kindly and clearly.

And hey, if you want, I can help you draft a follow-up message for any of those next steps. You don’t have to figure it all out alone.

You’re doing better than you think.
